title: Lost Procedures, GPS Navigation, and Diversion Decision-Making

required_knowledge_points.title: The 3C Lost Procedure — Climb, Circle, Communicate, Conserve
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE simulates a lost scenario and says 'You don't know where you are.' The applicant who says 'I'll turn on the GPS' has missed the pedagogical point — what if GPS is down or you've never confirmed your last known position? The 3C procedure is the airmanship-first answer.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: When positionally uncertain in VFR flight, execute the 3C Lost Procedure in sequence: (1) CLIMB: gaining altitude expands the visible horizon for landmark identification, improves VHF radio range to contact ATC or FSS, and extends GPS reception. New altitude must still clear obstacles per 91.119. (2) CIRCLE: orbit over the last known landmark to stop the progression of positional error. Do not continue flying in a random direction. (3) COMMUNICATE: squawk 7700 (emergency) or 7600 (radio failure, if applicable), then contact 121.5 MHz or nearest ATC. Announce: callsign, VFR uncertain of position, type, altitude, last known position, request assistance. (4) CONSERVE: set best-range power setting, avoid large course deviations that consume fuel while lost.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### 3C Lost Procedure — Execute In Order

**1. CLIMB**
- Altitude expands **visible horizon** for landmark identification
- Improves **VHF radio range** to ATC and FSS
- Extends **glide footprint** in case of engine failure
- Must still comply with **14 CFR 91.119** obstacle clearance

**2. CIRCLE**
- Orbit over the **last known landmark** — stop progressing the positional error
- Every additional mile of flight in a random direction **doubles the uncertainty**
- Do not navigate until position is confirmed

**3. COMMUNICATE**
- Squawk **7700** (emergency) or **7600** (radio failure)
- Contact **121.5 MHz** (emergency frequency) or nearest ATC facility
- Standard call: '[Callsign], [type], VFR uncertain of position, altitude [ALT], last known position [landmark], request assistance'
- ATC radar may **positively identify your transponder** and vector you immediately

**4. CONSERVE**
- Set **best-range power setting** to maximize remaining endurance
- Avoid large course deviations that consume fuel while the situation is unresolved

required_knowledge_points.title: Squawk Codes — 1200, 7700, 7600, 7500 and What Each Triggers
required_knowledge_points.why: A pilot who squawks 7700 instead of 7600 just declared an emergency instead of radio failure. A pilot who mistakenly squawks 7500 will be intercepted by fighter aircraft. The DPE tests code awareness under simulated stress: 'The radio just went dead — what do you squawk?'
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Transponder codes: (1) 1200 — VFR standard squawk in the United States. Set when operating VFR without ATC assignment. (2) 7700 — EMERGENCY (Mayday). Triggers ATC emergency response: priority handling, coordination with emergency services, airport crash equipment. (3) 7600 — RADIO FAILURE (NORDO). Signals two-way radio communication failure. ATC will watch for 7600 and support NORDO arrival procedures per 14 CFR 91.185. (4) 7500 — HIJACK. Triggers military intercept coordination. NEVER squawk 7500 unless under actual hijacking threat — ATC cannot rescind a 7500 squawk; the response is automatic. Memory: '75 = taken alive, 76 = radio sick, 77 = emergency heaven.'
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Transponder Emergency Codes — Quick Reference

| Code | Meaning | ATC Response | Use When |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1200** | VFR standard — no ATC assignment | Normal radar return | Operating VFR without a discrete code |
| **7700** | **EMERGENCY (Mayday)** | Emergency services, priority handling, crash equipment | Actual in-flight emergency |
| **7600** | **Radio Failure (NORDO)** | Airspace cleared for NORDO arrival (91.185) | Two-way radio failure |
| **7500** | **Hijack / Aircraft Seizure** | **Automatic military intercept** — cannot be verbally canceled | Only if aircraft is being seized |

### The 7500 Warning
- Squawking **7500 accidentally** (e.g., reaching for 7600) = **fighter intercept within minutes**
- ATC **cannot cancel** a 7500 response verbally — the protocol is automatic
- This is why deliberate code entry technique matters

### Memory Aid
- **75** = 'taken alive' (hijack)
- **76** = 'radio sick' (NORDO)
- **77** = 'emergency heaven'

required_knowledge_points.title: In-Flight Diversion — The Three-Step Decision Model
required_knowledge_points.why: The NTSB documents hundreds of accidents where pilots continued to a deteriorating destination rather than diverting when the decision was easy. VFR-into-IMC fatality rate is 11.2x higher than average (NTSB SS-15-01). The DPE simulates deteriorating weather at destination to test whether the applicant proactively diverts vs. waits until there is no good option.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Three-step diversion decision model: (1) IDENTIFY THE TRIGGER: predefine a personal trigger for diversion before flight, not in flight. Examples: ceiling drops below 2,000 feet at destination; fuel reaches final reserve; headwind exceeds 30 knots. Triggers set before flight remove in-flight cognitive load. (2) SELECT THE ALTERNATE: when trigger fires, stop and identify the best diversion airport. Selection criteria: sufficient runway length, fuel available, VFR conditions, no active SUA, reachable within fuel state. (3) NAVIGATE TO ALTERNATE: calculate direct heading and ETE from current position. If EFB is functional: direct-to. If not: use pilotage to identify compass bearing to alternate, apply wind correction, fly magnetic heading.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Three-Step Diversion Decision Model

**Step 1: Identify the Trigger (Before Takeoff)**
- Define a **personal diversion trigger** on the ground — not while airborne under stress
- Example triggers:
  - Ceiling at destination < **2,000 feet** at [waypoint]
  - Visibility at destination < **5 SM**
  - Fuel drops to **final reserve**
- Written triggers remove **plan continuation bias** — the psychological pressure to press on

**Step 2: Select the Alternate (When Trigger Fires)**
Airport selection criteria:
- Sufficient **runway length** for the aircraft
- **Fuel available** on field
- **VFR conditions** at field (confirm by METAR or phone)
- No active **SUA** on the direct route
- Reachable within **current fuel state**

**Step 3: Navigate to the Alternate**
- EFB available: **Direct-To** alternate
- EFB unavailable: pilotage → identify compass bearing from current landmark → apply WCA → fly magnetic heading
- **Amend or close** the original flight plan; activate a new one to the alternate

> **NTSB SS-15-01:** VFR-into-IMC fatality rate is **11.2x higher** than any other cause of fatal accidents in Part 91 GA

required_knowledge_points.title: GPS Navigation Principles — RAIM, ADS-B, and the WAAS Advantage
required_knowledge_points.why: A pilot who punches 'direct to' into a GPS without understanding RAIM alerts, WAAS limitations, or what the signal provides cannot safely evaluate GPS failures. The DPE increasingly tests GPS operation concepts as GA has migrated almost entirely to GPS navigation.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: GPS foundations for Part 91 VFR: (1) RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring): the GPS receiver's self-monitoring system that verifies satellite geometry is sufficient for reliable positioning. RAIM alert = insufficient satellites or quality for navigation integrity. Response: do not navigate by GPS; revert to pilotage or VOR. (2) WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System): FAA ground stations broadcast corrections improving GPS horizontal accuracy from ~100 feet (standard) to 3 meters or less (WAAS). Required for LPV approaches. (3) ADS-B Out: aircraft broadcast GPS-derived position on 978 MHz UAT (GA under 18,000 ft) or 1090 MHz Mode S. Required in most controlled airspace per 14 CFR 91.225. ADS-B In provides traffic and FIS-B weather. (4) Database currency per AC 90-100A: outdated database may show incorrect airspace boundaries, missing TFRs, or wrong frequencies.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### GPS Accuracy Systems

| System | What It Does | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| **Standard GPS** | Satellite-only positioning | ~100 feet horizontal |
| **WAAS** | Ground station corrections broadcast to aircraft | **~3 meters horizontal** |

### RAIM — Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring
- The GPS receiver's **self-monitoring system**
- Verifies **satellite geometry** is sufficient to provide reliable positioning
- **RAIM alert response:** Do NOT navigate by GPS; revert to **pilotage or VOR**

### ADS-B — Two-Way System
| Component | Direction | Provides |
|---|---|---|
| **ADS-B Out** | Aircraft → Ground/Air | GPS-derived position broadcast on 978 MHz (UAT) or 1090 MHz |
| **ADS-B In** | Ground → Aircraft | Traffic targets + **FIS-B weather** (NEXRAD, METARs, TFRs) |

- **ADS-B Out required** in Class A, B, C, and Mode C Veil airspace per **14 CFR 91.225**

### Database Currency (AC 90-100A)
- Outdated GPS database may display: **incorrect airspace boundaries**, **missing TFRs**, **wrong frequencies**
- Update databases **before every cross-country flight** — treat as a checklist item

lesson_overview:
## Lost Procedures, GPS Navigation, and Diversion — When the Plan Falls Apart

Every cross-country plan assumes things go correctly. They don't always. The METAR at the destination deteriorates. The GPS loses signal. You look up from the cockpit and realize the landmark you expected isn't where you thought it would be. The pilot who has pre-planned responses to these scenarios makes methodical decisions. The pilot who improvises under stress makes fatal ones.

**The 3C lost procedure — airmanship before technology.** When positional certainty fails, the instinctive reaction is often to keep flying while trying to figure out where you are. That's the wrong response — every mile of continued flight in the wrong direction doubles the positional error. The correct procedure, in order: (1) CLIMB — altitude extends radio range, expands the visible horizon, and extends the glide footprint. (2) CIRCLE — orbit over the last known landmark; stop progressing the error. (3) COMMUNICATE — squawk 7700 and call 121.5 MHz or the nearest ATC frequency; ATC radar may paint you immediately. (4) CONSERVE — set best-range power setting; don't burn fuel on large diversions until an alternate is confirmed. A student who says 'I'd just press Direct-To on the GPS' has answered with technology but failed the airmanship test.

**Squawk codes: the four that matter and the one you never accidentally select.** 1200 is the VFR default. 7700 declares an emergency — ATC coordinates emergency services and priority handling. 7600 is radio failure — ATC will watch for your code and support a NORDO arrival under 91.185. 7500 is hijack — the response is automatic and cannot be verbally canceled. A pilot who accidentally selects 7500 while reaching for 7600 will have fighters on their wing within minutes, regardless of radio explanation. Enter codes deliberately.

**Diversion decision-making: set the trigger before you need it.** The NTSB found that VFR-into-IMC accidents almost universally involved multiple early diversion opportunities that the pilot passed. Plan continuation bias is powerful. The defense: define your personal diversion triggers BEFORE takeoff. 'If ceiling at destination is below 2,000 feet when I reach this waypoint, I divert to [alternate].' Write it down. Commit to it. When the trigger fires, execute — don't renegotiate.

**GPS: RAIM, WAAS, ADS-B, and the currency trap.** RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) is the GPS receiver's self-check — a RAIM alert means the satellite geometry is insufficient for reliable positioning. Revert to pilotage or VOR. WAAS improves GPS accuracy from ~100 feet to ~3 meters using ground station corrections. ADS-B Out broadcasts GPS-derived position per 91.225 requirements. ADS-B In delivers traffic and FIS-B weather. An outdated GPS database may show incorrect airspace boundaries that were modified after the database was cut — pre-flight database verification is a checklist item.

**The checkride trap:** The DPE simulates a lost situation and says: 'Your GPS just failed, you're not sure of your position. What do you do?' The expected answer begins with the 3C framework — not 'I'd use my phone.' Then: 'What do you squawk?' 7700 for emergency. 'What if you have radio failure but know where you are?' 7600. 'What if you accidentally bump it to 7500?' That's the hijack scenario — and why deliberate code entry discipline matters.
